results.title: Marginal structural model - Wikipedia
results.content: # Marginal structural model. **Marginal structural models** are a class of statistical models used for causal inference in epidemiology. Such models handle the issue of time-dependent confounding in evaluation of the efficacy of interventions by inverse probability weighting for receipt of treatment, they allow us to estimate the average causal effects. The first marginal structural models were introduced in 2000. The works of James Robins, Babette Brumback, and Miguel Hernán provided an intuitive theory and an easy-to-implement software which made them popular for the analysis of longitudinal data. 1. **^** Robins, James; Hernán, Miguel; Brumback, Babette (September 2000). Title: Marginal Structural Models - data analysis - Datamethods Discussion Forum
# Marginal Structural Models. I am using a retrospective database to determine if on average the administration of lasix to racehorses prolongs their career. There is data on wether the horse received lasix for a particular start but the dose is not available. From a causal perspective the impact is thought to be that for each race the lasix prevents EIPH (exercise induced pulmonary hemorrhage) which ultimately leads to pulmonary fibrosis. The impact is not thought to be cumulative. If you look at percentage of starts using lasix the majority use it all the time. Using percentage lasix as the exposure seems futile as both the denominator and numerator are highly correlated with the outcome. In querying an AI bot on the best methodology for determining causality I received this response:. Implementation steps: a) Create inverse probability of treatment weights (IPTW):. b) Fit a weighted regression model:. c) Use robust standard errors to account for the weighting process. Marginal structural Cox models (MSM) provide the marginal causal relation between a time-varying exposure and a survival outcome (e.g. in this case, end of racing career), controlling for time-varying confounders without conditioning on those variables. An example in veterinary medicine is given in a 2017 Prev Vet Med paper on mastitis and culling risk in dairy cows. Maybe it would be good to start with defining a directed acyclic graph to help you model your thoughts (). Maybe something like this,where EIPH is the exposure and Lasix treatment a confounding factor:. I think the DAG is exactly the place to start. results.content:
Title: panel data - Estimating Marginal Structural Models with the {WeightIt} Package - Cross Validated
### more stack exchange communities. # [Estimating Marginal Structural Models with the {WeightIt} Package [closed]](/questions/669340/estimating-marginal-structural-models-with-the-weightit-package). I am used to using the {ipw} R package for estimating marginal structural models. Both the exposure $X$ and outcome $Y$ are time-varying and are both impacted by prior exposure, outcome, 3 time-varying confounders ($C\_1$, $C\_2$, $C\_3$) and 3 time-invariant confounders ($V\_1$, $V\_2$, and $V\_3$). I (think) I will be able to get weights that allow me to estimate an "unbiased" contemporaneous $X$ effect that accounts for time-varying confounding and exposure-outcome feedback loops. I think I would also be able to estimate the 1-time period lagged effect of $X$ as well but I'm not sure. As for the {WeightI} package, I'm still confused since, because the data has to be cast wide, `X_1` refers to the value of $X$ in a specific time period rather than $X$ at time $t$. For example, if I'm interested in estimating the effect of $X\_{t-2}$ will I need to manually specify $C1\_{t-t-2}$, $C2\_{t, t-1, t-2}$, $C3\_{t, t-1, t-2}$, $V1\_{t, t-1, t-2}$, $V2\_{t-, t-1, t-2}$, $V3\_{t, t-1, t-2}$, $X\_{t, t-1}$, $Y\_{t, t-1}$? (2001) are for estimating the *joint* effect of multiple treatments (administered in sequence) on an outcome at a single, final time point. They estimate the contemporaneous effect of treatment on an outcome (possibly with lagged treatments included), adjusting for confounding by prior time points. This allows one to use a single model for the weights that is applied at each time point, which includes the covariates from the most recent time point and a fixed number of lagged time points. This type of design is used for time series cross-sectional data, which is what you have (many time points), whereas traditional MSMs are used with fewer time points to explore specific treatment histories. So, `ipw()` facilitates estimation of repeated measures MSMs, and `WeightIt` facilitates estimation of traditional MSMs. The methods, typical modeling assumptions, estimands, and data types differ quite a bit between the two, which is why there seems to be a disconnect between the two packages. Marginal Structural Models to Estimate the Joint Causal Effect of Nonrandomized Treatments. Estimating the causal effect of zidovudine on CD4 count with a marginal structural model for repeated measures.
